historyReviewBoundary: All 115 histories have author source checks. Final independent review covered metadata and numerical checks for all 115 classes, 12 deeper class targets and source-gap samples in seven classes. It did not independently verify every passage of every cited source.

history.name: Cardiac glycosides

starting.description: A reported multi-herb remedy for dropsy led Withering to identify foxglove as the likely active plant and investigate its effects in patients. Later, reported greater physiological activity of D. lanata than the medicinal D. purpurea prompted Smith to fractionate the former's glucosides, yielding digoxin.

inspiration.description: Reported clinical effects of a multi-herb recipe, subsequent observed effects of foxglove, and the reported physiological activity of D. lanata that motivated Smith's later comparative isolation.

steps.description: Withering learned of a reported dropsy remedy and inferred that foxglove was its active ingredient.

He reported diuresis and other clinical observations with foxglove, adjusted its preparation and dosing in response to variable activity and toxicity, and suggested a possible therapeutic use for its effect on heart motion.

Later reports that D. lanata had greater physiological activity than the medicinal D. purpurea prompted Smith to fractionate its glucosides; he isolated and named digoxin and described an animal bioassay.
A historical analysis reports that the MRC committee agreed in 1931 to Wayne's clinical testing of purified glycosides, including oral digoxin; it reports ventricular-rate slowing and oral activity.

design.description: Withering refined preparation and dosing; Smith deliberately fractionated and characterized active plant glucosides and reported a bioassay of the isolated digoxin. These are preparation and isolation, not evidence of a designed new molecular scaffold.

circumstances.description: Withering's later testing and preparation refinement and Smith's comparative fractionation were deliberate; the circumstances of the earlier folk discovery are not established.

limits: The directly traced branch is digitalis, from plant preparations to the isolation of digoxin from a second foxglove species; non-digitalis plant sources require separate historical evidence.
conflicts: A later advertisement named the reported woman and pictured a direct payment; Krikler (E10) identifies those as embellishments, whereas Withering's own account (E1–E2) reports only what he was told. Her identity and the earlier remedy's outcome are not independently established.
gaps: Smith's cited Wokes 1929 comparison has not been independently read.
Wayne's 1933 clinical report was located in Toth's reference list but its original text and a verified direct URL were not obtained; clinical testing is reported through Toth's retrospective account.
Smith's article was read through the search service's extracted PDF text; direct local retrieval and PDF screenshots failed, so no local copy was obtained.
The original woman and her remedy have not been independently authenticated; Krikler's analysis of the later advertisement is secondary and the advertisement was not independently inspected.

humanContributionInterpretation.summary: A reported dropsy remedy and subsequent patient diuresis and pulse changes directed Withering's foxglove investigation.
humanContributionInterpretation.scope: The later isolation of digoxin used bioassays; this is an ancestral clinical lineage, not an independent origin for every glycoside.
